origen: Independently reconstructed from the robot published by MIT CSAIL. Technical demonstration; not an original design, and it uses no MIT photographs.

conjuntos.subtitulo: Dome · three elements · iris · seals · sensor
conjuntos.descripcion: Sealed optics in the nose: a pressure dome, a three-element train with its iris and the sensor at the back, all behind two O-rings. This is how the fish sees, and the reason it exists: getting close to wildlife that flees any conventional submersible.

Everything that has to stay dry: control boards, microcontroller, LiPo batteries and the wiring that runs back to the tail. It lives in the rigid section because that is the only part that does not deform while swimming.

They do not propel: they steer. They deflect together to pitch and in opposite directions to help the turn, like the ailerons of an aircraft. Each one carries its own sealed servo with horn and pushrod.

conjuntos.subtitulo: Pump · ballast cylinder · hoses · bulkhead fittings
conjuntos.descripcion: Two uses of water in the same machine. The pump sends it to two chambers moulded inside the silicone of the tail: fill the one on one side, that half swells and the soft body curves toward the other. There is no shaft and no connecting rod, which is why it swims without the wake or the noise of a propeller. The ballast cylinder does the other job: a leadscrew drives a piston that changes the displaced volume, and with it the fish rises or sinks without pushing against anything. Changing depth costs energy; holding it does not.

conjuntos.subtitulo: Rigid shell · silicone skin · fins · bulkhead
conjuntos.descripcion: The front half is a rigid watertight shell; the rear half is silicone skin. That boundary is the whole idea: a soft body undulates instead of hinging, which is why it swims without the noise or the wake of a propeller.

conjuntos.subtitulo: Ribs · spine · dorsal spar · caudal fin
conjuntos.descripcion: Ribs, spine and dorsal spar. The wave travels down the chain from front to back with a progressive phase — each rib lags slightly behind the one before it — and it is that travelling wave, not the slap of the fin, that produces thrust.
